definition: The statement $\mathrm{H}_0$ assumed true during a hypothesis test, such as no association, no difference between population means, or data fitting a claimed distribution; a test either rejects it or does not, and never proves it.
The statement $\mathrm{H}_1$ that a test finds evidence for when it rejects $\mathrm{H}_0$; its form ($\neq$, or $>$ or $<$) decides whether a t-test is two-tailed or one-tailed.
The probability threshold, such as $5\%$, chosen before a hypothesis test: $\mathrm{H}_0$ is rejected when the p-value is less than it.

The probability, assuming $\mathrm{H}_0$ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ when it is less than the significance level. It is not the probability that $\mathrm{H}_0$ is true.

The count predicted for a category if $\mathrm{H}_0$ is true, compared with the observed (recorded) count; in a contingency table it is row total × column total ÷ grand total, and a χ² test needs each one greater than $5$.
A two-way table of observed frequencies, with one categorical variable in the rows and another in the columns, used in the χ² test for independence.

The number of values free to vary once the totals are fixed: $(r - 1)(c - 1)$ for a contingency table with $r$ rows and $c$ columns, and $n - 1$ for an SL goodness of fit test with $n$ categories (one fewer for each parameter estimated from the data).
A test of $\mathrm{H}_0$: two categorical variables are independent, using a contingency table; it uses the upper tail only and needs every expected frequency greater than $5$.

A test of $\mathrm{H}_0$: observed frequencies fit a claimed distribution; with $n$ categories and no parameters estimated from the data it has $n - 1$ degrees of freedom, uses the upper tail only and needs every expected frequency greater than $5$.
A test about population means using the t-distribution; at SL it is the pooled two-sample t-test, for unpaired samples from normal populations with unknown but equal variances.
A test whose $\mathrm{H}_1$ states a direction, such as $\mu_1 > \mu_2$, so the p-value is the area in one tail only.
A test whose $\mathrm{H}_1$ uses $\neq$, such as $\mu_1 \neq \mu_2$, so the p-value counts results as extreme in both tails.
